hook.text: The standard deviation and the standard error get mixed up all the time. Both measure a spread... just not of the same thing.

sd.text: Take two hundred customers' ages. Their standard deviation is the spread of the data: about ten and a half years.

move.text: But their average came from one sample. Ask two hundred different people... and it moves.

se.text: How far it moves is the standard error: the spread of the estimate, the width of its sampling distribution.

one.text: [curious] So how can you measure that, when you've only ever seen one average?

divide.text: Divide the standard deviation by the square root of the sample size.

numbers.text: Ten point five eight, over the square root of two hundred, gives zero point seven five.

contrast.text: The ages spread over decades. Their average wobbles by less than a year.

check.text: That's a bold claim from one sample, so let's check it.

pop.text: Here's a population with a spread of twenty-five. Draw fifty values, and average them.

repeat.text: Then do it again... ten thousand times.

pile.text: The averages pile up, with a spread of three point five.

match.text: From one sample, the shortcut said three point seven. Close, without repeating anything.

cost.text: Now, what does that square root cost?

curve.text: When data spreads by twenty, a hundred people give a standard error of two.

four.text: Halving it takes four hundred. Halving it again, sixteen hundred.

hundred.text: A tenth of the error takes a HUNDRED times the data. Precision gets expensive, fast.

ruler.text: So why does this number matter so much? It's the ruler the rest of inference measures with.

times.text: A hundred and twenty conversion times average eight point two seconds, with a standard error of zero point two two.

interval.text: Step about two standard errors either way, and you get seven point eight to eight point six. That's a confidence interval.

test.text: And a test counts how many standard errors an estimate sits from the value it's testing.

next.text: Next, we'll build that interval properly.
